chunks: Design constraints across industries. The question: What are some system design constraints in consumer electronics vs automotive vs aerospace/space/defense vs medical devices?
The same circuit gets designed differently depending on what happens if it fails and who pays for it.
A phone, a car, a spacecraft and a medical device might all use the same power-converter circuit.
The difference is the parts you choose, how far you stay under their limits, the testing you do, and the paperwork you keep.
Think of building a bridge for different uses. A garden footbridge can be cheap, and a wobble is no disaster. A highway bridge must last decades in all weather.
A bridge on a remote mountain pass, where nobody can ever repair it, needs extra strength everywhere.
A bridge over a hospital's emergency entrance needs inspections and records for every bolt. The stakes decide how careful you are.
failure acceleration climbs steeply with temperature.

A device run at 125 degrees Celsius ages about 78 times faster than at 55 degrees Celsius, which is why automotive and aerospace derate junction temperature and why high-temperature operating life (HTOL) tests are used to qualify parts.
Drag E a up to 1. 0 eV and the 125 degrees Celsius factor grows from about 78 to about 500; drag it down to 0. 4 eV and it shrinks to about 12.
Moving the reference down to 25 degrees Celsius raises it to about 940.
Derating: running a part well below its rated voltage, current or temperature so it lasts longer.
Qualified part: a part tested to a standard, such as AEC-Q for cars, that shows it survives harsh conditions.
Functional safety: processes and checks that keep a failure from hurting anyone. Radiation: high-energy particles in space that can flip memory bits or damage chips.
Leakage current: a tiny current that could flow through a person touching the equipment. Medical devices limit it very strictly.
Take one voltage converter. In a phone, you pick the cheapest part that meets spec, because a small failure rate costs less than over-engineering millions of units.
In a car, you pick a part qualified from -40 to 125 degrees C and add protection against a rough 12 volts supply, because it must last 10 to 15 years.
On a satellite, nobody can repair it, so you derate heavily and use radiation-tolerant parts.
In a medical device, you add isolation (an electrical barrier so almost no current can reach the patient) and keep records. That is the whole idea.
"The same circuit is designed differently because failure costs differ. Consumer is driven by cost, size and battery life with commercial parts and EMC marks.
Automotive adds minus 40 to 125 degrees, 10 to 15 year life, a rough 12 volt supply with load dump, AEC-Q parts and ISO 26262.
Aerospace, space and defense add radiation, vacuum, shock, no repair and heavy screening and documentation.
Medical is dominated by patient safety: IEC 60601 leakage and isolation limits, risk management and traceability."
